# Is a rainwater tank worth it for your garden?

*Test fixture written for this repo. The numbers are illustrative.*

A rainwater tank collects water from your roof so you can use it in the garden instead of tap water. How much it collects depends on your roof, your rainfall and the size of the tank.

As a rule of thumb, every square metre of roof collects about one litre of water for every millimetre of rain, minus some loss to gutters and first-flush diverters, typically around 20%. A 100 square metre roof in a place with 600 millimetres of rain a year can collect roughly 48,000 litres a year.

The catch is timing. Rain does not fall evenly. In a wet month the tank overflows and the extra water is lost. In a dry summer the garden takes water out faster than rain puts it in, and the tank runs empty. A typical garden in summer uses around 200 litres a day when watered by hand.

So tank size matters. A small 2,000 litre tank fills and overflows in a single big storm and can be empty within ten dry days. A 10,000 litre tank lasts most of a dry spell, but costs more and takes up space. Many owners find a tank of 5,000 litres is a good middle ground for a small garden.

People often think a tank will cover all their garden watering. In most places it covers the wet months easily and runs dry in exactly the weeks you need it most.

Tanks also need a pump, cleaning, and in some areas a permit.
